content: Heart sounds are the noises produced by the beating heart and the flow of blood through its chambers and valves. These sounds, often referred to as the heartbeat, are critical in assessing cardiac function. During cardiac auscultation, a stethoscope is used to listen to these sounds, which provide valuable information about the heart's condition. In healthy adults, there are two primary heart sounds, commonly described as lub and dub (or dup), which occur sequentially with each heartbeat. The first heart sound (S1) is caused by the closure of the atrioventricular (AV) valves (mitral and tricuspid valves) at the beginning of ventricular contraction (systole). The second heart sound (S2) is produced by the closure of the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary valves) at the start of ventricular relaxation (diastole). These sounds are the result of vibrations within the blood and surrounding structures as the valves close. In addition to these normal heart sounds, other sounds may be present, such as heart murmurs and adventitious sounds. Heart murmurs are caused by turbulent blood flow, which can occur either within or outside the heart. Murmurs may be classified as physiological (benign) or pathological (abnormal). Abnormal murmurs can result from conditions such as valve stenosis, which restricts the opening of a heart valve and creates turbulence, or valve insufficiency (regurgitation), which allows blood to flow backward when the valve fails to close properly. The timing and location of murmurs within the cardiac cycle depend on their underlying cause. First Heart Sound (S1) The first heart sound, or S1, is generated by the sudden cessation of reverse blood flow due to the closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the onset of systole. As ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, the inflow of venous blood into the ventricles is abruptly halted, causing the valve leaflets to close and preventing regurgitation of blood back into the atria. The S1 sound is primarily associated with the vibrations within the blood and surrounding structures as the valves close. Second Heart Sound (S2) The second heart sound, or S2, occurs at the beginning of diastole when the aortic and pulmonary valves close. As the left ventricle empties, its pressure falls below that of the aorta, causing a brief reversal of aortic blood flow that catches the aortic valve leaflets and forces them to close. Similarly, the pulmonary valve closes when the right ventricular pressure falls below that of the pulmonary artery. The S2 sound is also caused by vibrations within the blood and surrounding structures during this sudden cessation of flow. Splitting of the Second Heart Sound Physiologic Splitting: During inspiration, negative intrathoracic pressure increases venous return to the right side of the heart, delaying pulmonary valve closure (P2) relative to aortic valve closure (A2). This results in a physiologic splitting of S2. During expiration, the interval between A2 and P2 shortens, and the sounds may merge. Persistent Splitting: Persistent splitting of S2 is observed in conditions such as right bundle branch block (RBBB) and pulmonary hypertension, where delayed pulmonary valve closure occurs during both inspiration and expiration. Paradoxical Splitting: In left bundle branch block (LBBB), aortic stenosis, or severe heart failure, delayed aortic valve closure causes the pulmonic component (P2) to precede the aortic component (A2). This splitting is more apparent during expiration. Fixed Splitting: Fixed splitting of S2, which does not vary with respiration, is typically caused by atrial septal defects (ASD) or ventricular septal defects (VSD). These defects create a left-to-right shunt, increasing blood flow to the right heart and delaying pulmonary valve closure. Third Heart Sound (S3) The third heart sound, or S3, occurs during early diastole, shortly after S2. It is caused by vibrations resulting from the rapid filling of a non-compliant left ventricle. S3 is often described as having a cadence similar to the word Kentucky. While it can be a normal finding in individuals under 40 years of age, its presence in older adults is usually indicative of heart failure or other pathological conditions. S3 is best heard with the bell of the stethoscope and is also known as a ventricular gallop. Fourth Heart Sound (S4) The fourth heart sound, or S4, occurs just before S1, during late diastole, and is associated with atrial contraction. It is never considered normal and is indicative of a stiff or hypertrophic left ventricle. S4 is often described as having a cadence similar to the word Tennessee. It is best heard at the cardiac apex and becomes more apparent with maneuvers such as exercise or breath-holding. S4 is also referred to as a presystolic gallop or atrial gallop. Gallop Rhythms A gallop rhythm refers to the presence of additional heart sounds (S3 or S4) alongside the normal S1 and S2 sounds. When both S3 and S4 are present, it is termed a quadruple gallop. At rapid heart rates, S3 and S4 may merge into a single sound, known as a summation gallop. Heart Murmurs Heart murmurs are caused by turbulent blood flow and are often described as a whooshing sound. They can result from conditions such as valve regurgitation, valve stenosis, or abnormal openings between heart chambers. The intensity and characteristics of murmurs can vary with the severity of the underlying condition. For example: Mitral Regurgitation: The most common murmur, often loud and easily detected. Aortic Stenosis: A systolic ejection murmur, more common in older adults or those with a bicuspid aortic valve. Aortic Regurgitation: A high-pitched murmur, though often difficult to detect without advanced equipment. Mitral Stenosis: A low-frequency rumbling murmur, best heard with a high-quality stethoscope. Adventitious Sounds Clicks: High-pitched sounds caused by conditions such as mitral valve prolapse or bicuspid aortic valve. Rubs: Pericardial friction rubs, associated with pericarditis, produce a scratching or creaking sound due to the rubbing of inflamed pericardial layers. Recording Heart Sounds Modern electronic stethoscopes allow for the recording and playback of heart sounds, enabling detailed analysis and diagnosis of murmurs and other abnormal sounds. These recordings can be used to faithfully reproduce low-frequency murmurs and other subtle cardiac sounds. Surface Anatomy and Auscultation Heart sounds are best heard at specific locations downstream from the valves, where the blood flow and vibrations are most prominent. These locations can be remembered using the mnemonic All The President’s Men: Aortic Area: Right second intercostal space. Pulmonic Area: Left second intercostal space. Tricuspid Area: Left fourth intercostal space at the sternal border. Mitral Area: Fifth intercostal space, lateral to the left midclavicular line. In summary, heart sounds and murmurs provide critical insights into cardiac function and pathology. Advances in auscultation techniques and diagnostic tools, such as echocardiography, have significantly enhanced the ability to evaluate and manage cardiac conditions.
